notes.meaning: God commands Moses to lead a final battle against the Midianites to punish them for leading Israel into sin. The Midianites had lured the people into worshiping idols and committing sexual sins at Peor. After completing this final assignment from the Lord, Moses will die and be reunited with his ancestors.

Moses promptly relays the command to the people, telling them to equip men for battle. Although God called it vengeance for Israel, Moses describes it as the Lord's vengeance, showing that sin against God's people is an offense against God Himself. The soldiers were sent out to carry out God's righteous judgment rather than personal revenge.

Each of the twelve tribes provides one thousand soldiers, making a modest army of twelve thousand men. This equal draft united the whole nation in the conflict and prevented jealousy among the tribes. The small force also required the people to trust God for the victory instead of relying on their own numbers.

Moses sends the army into battle accompanied by Phinehas, the priest known for his zeal in turning away God's wrath at Peor. Phinehas brings the sacred trumpets used to blow alarms and call on the Lord for help during conflict. His presence marked this campaign as a holy conflict directed by God rather than an ordinary war.

The Israelite force attacks the local Midianite settlements and kills every adult fighting man who opposes them. This victory broke the local military strength of the enemy confederation. God granted them complete success over the Midianite forces in that area just as He had promised.

The soldiers execute the five ruling chiefs of the Midianite region alongside their men. They also kill Balaam, who had come back among these enemies after failing to curse Israel. God's providence brought Balaam to justice for plotting the ruin of God's people.

Following standard ancient warfare practices, the soldiers take the surviving women and children as prisoners. They also seize all the cattle, flocks, and household wealth of the defeated settlements. The troops gather this immense wealth to bring back to the Israelite camp.

The troops set fire to the Midianite towns and temporary camps, completely wiping out their bases and idol shrines. They collect all the captured livestock, people, and valuable goods to carry back. This prevented any surviving enemies from quickly rebuilding or reoccupying the territory.

The army brings the captives and all the plunder back to the main Israelite camp on the plains of Moab across from Jericho. Instead of dividing the spoils immediately for themselves, they present everything to Moses, Eleazar the high priest, and the leaders. This showed their submission to God's appointed authorities.

Moses, Eleazar, and the tribal leaders go out to meet the returning soldiers outside the camp borders. They went out to honor the army for its victory, but also to stop them from entering the community while still ceremonially unclean from the dead. This maintained the purity required around the dwelling place of God.

Moses becomes very angry with the army commanders returning from the battlefield. Despite their military victory, they had failed to carry out the Lord's full judgment on the instigators of sin. Faithful leaders must confront mistakes even in the middle of a celebration.

Moses rebukes the commanders for sparing the Midianite women who were the direct cause of Israel's fall at Peor. It was these very women who had acted on Balaam's wicked advice to seduce Israel into sexual sin and idol worship, bringing a deadly plague on God's people. Sparing them brought a terrible moral and spiritual hazard right back into the camp.

Moses orders the death of every young boy and every woman who had been intimate with a man. The mature women were guilty of enticing Israel into idolatry, and leaving the young boys would allow the corrupted Midianite clans to rebuild and seek revenge later. God, as the supreme author of life, executed a severe judicial sentence against a nation that sought Israel's destruction.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical critics view this story as a later legend created to reflect early war ideals, while others see it as a factual ancient account of severe tribal warfare commanded under the theocratic order.

notes.meaning: The soldiers are permitted to spare the young unmarried girls who had taken no part in the seduction at Peor. These young women could be taken into Israelite households as servants or later married under biblical laws. Because they were innocent of the crimes at Peor, they could be safely integrated into the faith and life of Israel.

notes.meaning: Anyone who killed an enemy or touched a corpse had to stay outside the camp for seven days to undergo ritual cleansing. They were required to wash themselves and their captives on the third and seventh days using the water of purification. Every piece of clothing, leather, goat's hair, and wooden article taken from the enemy also had to be cleansed from the defilement of death.

Eleazar the high priest steps forward to deliver the specific priestly laws of cleansing to the soldiers. As priest, his role was to teach and enforce ritual cleanliness according to the law given to Moses. He provides clear directions on how different kinds of booty must be purified before entering the camp.

Metals like gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, and lead had to pass through fire because they could withstand heat. Afterward, they were still sprinkled with the special cleansing water made with the ashes of the red heifer. Items that could not survive fire were washed thoroughly in water so that every trace of past pagan use was wiped away.

On the seventh day, the soldiers must wash their clothes to complete their purification. Once they are ceremonially clean, they are welcomed back into the camp and into fellowship with the rest of Israel. God required this delay to remind the nation of the solemn cost of human life and the holiness of His presence.

The Lord instructs Moses, Eleazar, and the clan leaders to count all the captured people and livestock accurately. The plunder is to be split into two equal halves: one half for the twelve thousand soldiers who faced the dangers of combat, and the other half for the rest of the congregation who stayed behind. This fair system honored the brave soldiers while ensuring that the whole community shared in the blessing.
